entries.name: Vale Ventures IA LLC v. Gray Jay Management Investments, LLC,

arguments_rejected_or_waived: Payoff Letter as acceleration: rejected. The VPN separately addresses prepayment (§ 2.03(a), a borrower right) and acceleration (§ 7.02(a), a lender remedy requiring notice declaring the note due and payable). The Repayment Notice did not alter maturity, and the OWL Lender never declared acceleration, so the repayment was a prepayment. The Court also rejected Gray Jay's points that the notice was not "irrevocable" and that only Vale, not PWS on its behalf, could prepay (fn. 188).

Prevention doctrine excusing the lack of acceleration: rejected. No ECL or VPN provision required Vale to disclose the Pilot Transaction's terms. Giving NGP extra advance notice did not breach § 2.03(a). The record shows the OWL Lender would not have accelerated in any event, and the prevention doctrine does not apply where the condition would not have occurred regardless. The Court also rejected Gray Jay's quibbles about how the notice was addressed, given actual notice and the OWL Lender's signed acknowledgment (fn. 203).

Balance-sheet insolvency: rejected. The slide deck improperly compared debt with an enterprise fair-market-value figure, and under Quadrant a positive value means the firm is solvent; the same deck showed nine-figure implied equity values. On the Madera Event, the Court adopted the probable-and-reasonably-estimable standard and found the liability neither probable nor estimable at the time. Post-2023 OCD materials were of questionable relevance, the Lonquist analysis found any plume far from water wells, and Gray Jay's expert Kronkosky, who did not testify, was given no weight. The Court assumed arguendo that subsidiary remediation costs could reach Vale (fn. 232).

Cash-flow insolvency: rejected. Hines's testimony about past-due vendors lacked contemporaneous support such as missed payments, demand letters or liens. Good-faith negotiation with creditors is not insolvency, and the maturing debt was in fact repaid through the Pilot Transaction.

Prior material breach of the implied covenant: the gap-filler theory may have been abandoned when Gray Jay pivoted at oral argument, and it fails anyway because the ECL and VPN address dispositions without prohibiting the Pilot Transaction. Dieckman was distinguished. The discretion-based theory was waived because it was not raised in the post-trial brief, which Gray Jay admitted. It also fails on the merits because no contract term gives Vale relevant discretion, and structuring around contractual restrictions is not bad faith (fn. 279).

Frustration of purpose: rejected. The ECL's purpose was to facilitate Gray Jay's investment as part of the broader Transaction, and the parties allocated the foreseeable risk of a disposition through the default-and-acceleration condition. Gray Jay's requested adverse inference that Vale structured the deal to avoid the ECL conditions was denied as moot, because Vale concedes that fact and it does not show bad faith.

Gray Jay's opposition to specific performance of the ECL investment obligation: waived. Gray Jay opposed only the capital-call request, not the order to purchase securities. The Court added that specific performance of a purchase of stock in a privately held entity is independently supportable (fn. 322).

Vale's implied covenant claim (Count II): waived because it was omitted from Vale's opening post-trial brief. It also fails on the merits because the ECL's pricing term expressly addresses Gray Jay's purchase obligation if Vale's value declines.

Order directing Gray Jay to issue a capital call: denied. The ECL's non-recourse clause bars remedies against Gray Jay's managers and members. The Court will not dictate how a judgment is satisfied, and Vale is not a party to the Gray Jay LLC Agreement. Vale also did not invoke 6 Del. C. § 18-502(b) (fn. 329).

Damages for interest on the Oceanides Promissory Note: denied. Vale waived any response to Gray Jay's invocation of the ECL damages cap, and the $10 million cap leaves no room for further recovery. The Court did not decide whether these damages are consequential and therefore excluded, though it said Gray Jay "seemingly has a strong argument" that they are.

authorities_cited.authority: Equity Commitment Letter (ECL) (termination conditions; non-recourse clause; $10 million liability cap; consequential damages exclusion; pricing term)
authorities_cited.proposition: Gray Jay's obligation terminates only upon enumerated events, including default and acceleration of the VPN or Vale's insolvency. The non-recourse clause bars relief against Gray Jay's managers and members, and the cap limits Gray Jay's maximum liability to $10 million less prior purchases.

authorities_cited.authority: Vendor Promissory Note (VPN) §§ 2.03(a), 6.02, 7.01, 7.02(a)
authorities_cited.proposition: Prepayment requires an irrevocable Repayment Notice at least five Business Days in advance. Acceleration for non-§ 7.01(f) defaults requires lender notice declaring the note due and payable, and the meaningful variation between the two provisions shows notice was material.

authorities_cited.authority: Desktop Metal, Inc. v. Nano Dimension Ltd., 2025 WL 904521 (Del. Ch. Mar. 24, 2025) (quoting AB Stable VIII, LLC v. Maps Hotels and Resorts One LLC, 2020 WL 7024929 (Del. Ch. Nov. 30, 2020))
authorities_cited.proposition: The party seeking to avoid an obligation bears the burden of proving a condition that extinguishes the duty to perform.

authorities_cited.authority: Black's Law Dictionary (12th ed. 2024) ("Prepayment Clause"; "Acceleration")
authorities_cited.proposition: Prepayment satisfies a debt before its due date, while acceleration advances the maturity date so the entire debt is due immediately.

authorities_cited.authority: Snow Phipps Gp., LLC v. KCake Acq., Inc., 2021 WL 1714202 (Del. Ch. Apr. 30, 2021)
authorities_cited.proposition: The prevention doctrine requires that the preventing act breach a contractual duty. Specific performance requires clear and convincing evidence. Contractual remedy limits may bear on prejudgment interest that accompanies specific performance.

authorities_cited.authority: Quadrant Structured Prods. Co., Ltd. v. Vertin, 2015 WL 6157759 (Del. Ch. Oct. 20, 2015) (also 102 A.3d 155 (Del. Ch. 2014))
authorities_cited.proposition: The balance-sheet test asks what a buyer would pay for the debtor's entire package of assets and liabilities, and a positive price means the firm is solvent.

authorities_cited.authority: In re Geneius Biotechnology, Inc., 2017 WL 6209593 (Del. Ch. Dec. 8, 2017)
authorities_cited.proposition: Cash-flow insolvency is not shown absent defaults, judgments, liens or an inability to raise capital, and good-faith negotiation with creditors is not enough.

authorities_cited.authority: Johnson & Johnson v. Fortis Advisors LLC, 352 A.3d 229 (Del. 2026)
authorities_cited.proposition: The gap-filler implied covenant cannot contradict express terms or cover developments that could have been anticipated. Its discretion variant requires a contractual grant of discretion over a central aspect of the bargain.

authorities_cited.authority: Wilm. Sav. Fund Soc'y, FSB v. Foresight Energy LLC, 2015 WL 7889552 (Del. Ch. Dec. 4, 2015)
authorities_cited.proposition: Efforts to structure a transaction to avoid tripping contractual terms are permissible, and sophisticated parties can draft against evasion.

authorities_cited.authority: Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. v. AIG Life Ins. Co., 901 A.2d 106 (Del. 2006), aff'g 2005 WL 5757652 (Del. Ch. Apr. 1, 2005)
authorities_cited.proposition: Frustration of purpose excuses performance only where the principal purpose is substantially frustrated by an unforeseeable event, and it does not apply where the event was reasonably foreseeable and could have been provided for.

authorities_cited.authority: Emerald P'rs v. Berlin, 726 A.2d 1215 (Del. 1999)
authorities_cited.proposition: Issues not briefed are deemed waived. Applied to Gray Jay's non-response on breach, on specific performance of the ECL and on costs, and to Vale's non-response on the damages cap.

authorities_cited.authority: Beard Rsch., Inc. v. Kates, 981 A.2d 1175 (Del. Ch. 2009)
authorities_cited.proposition: Negligent failure to preserve evidence supports monetary sanctions; applied to award Gray Jay its spoliation-motion fees.

authorities_cited.authority: Dieckman v. Regency GP LP, 155 A.3d 358 (Del. 2017)
authorities_cited.proposition: An implied term must be so obvious that the parties failed to express it only because it went without saying; Gray Jay instead sought to extend existing restrictions.

authorities_cited.authority: Twin Willows, LLC v. Pritzkur, 2022 WL 3039775 (Del. Ch. Aug. 2, 2022)
authorities_cited.proposition: The prevention doctrine does not apply if the condition would not have occurred regardless of the other party's conduct.

authorities_cited.authority: Oxbow Carbon & Mins. Hldgs., Inc. v. Crestview-Oxbow Acq., LLC, 202 A.3d 482 (Del. 2019)
authorities_cited.proposition: An issue not raised in post-trial briefing is waived.

authorities_cited.authority: In re IBP, Inc. S'holders Litig., 789 A.2d 14 (Del. Ch. 2001)
authorities_cited.proposition: Failure to raise a claim in the opening brief waives it.

authorities_cited.authority: Gandhi-Kapoor v. Hone Capital LLC, 305 A.3d 707 (Del. Ch. 2023)
authorities_cited.proposition: The Court will not deploy coercive remedies to dictate how a judgment debtor performs.

authorities_cited.authority: Florida Chem. Co., LLC v. Flotek Indus., Inc., 262 A.3d 1066 (Del. Ch. 2021)
authorities_cited.proposition: Only a party to a contract has standing to enforce it.

authorities_cited.authority: LG Elecs. Inc. v. Invention Inv. Fund I, L.P., 362 A.3d 1266 (Del. 2026)
authorities_cited.proposition: Delaware courts enforce contractual damages caps, and prejudgment interest has been awarded on top of a cap.

authorities_cited.authority: Kaung v. Cole Nat. Corp., 884 A.2d 500 (Del. 2005)
authorities_cited.proposition: The bad-faith exception to the American Rule applies to vexatious, wanton or oppressive litigation conduct.

authorities_cited.authority: Jeffery v. Seven Seventeen Corp., 461 A.2d 1009 (Del. 1983)
authorities_cited.proposition: An acceleration clause exists solely to protect the lender.

authorities_cited.authority: Gildor v. Optical Solutions, Inc., 2006 WL 4782348 (Del. Ch. June 5, 2006)
authorities_cited.proposition: Specific performance of a stock purchase is appropriate where the stock is unique or not available in the market (fn. 322).
Costs are awarded to the prevailing party.
Not invoked by Vale as a basis to compel member contributions as a creditor (fn. 329).

authorities_cited.authority: Restatement (Second) of Contracts §§ 245, 265, 358
authorities_cited.proposition: Sources for the prevention doctrine, frustration of purpose and damages for delay accompanying specific performance.

summary.brief_summary: Vale, an Instar vehicle, sued Gray Jay, the investment entity of OWL's former executives, to enforce Gray Jay's ECL commitment to invest in Vale as the VPN was repaid; PWS repaid the VPN in full in the Pilot Transaction, which Vale structured downstream of Vale to avoid the ECL's termination triggers. After trial, Vice Chancellor Cook held that Gray Jay breached and bore, but failed to carry, the burden of proving a termination event. Payoff by Repayment Notice was a prepayment, not an acceleration, and Gray Jay offered no credible evidence of balance-sheet or cash-flow insolvency, including from the Madera Event. The Court rejected Gray Jay's implied covenant and frustration defenses because the parties allocated disposition risk through the default-and-acceleration condition and structuring around contract terms is not bad faith, and it ordered specific performance of the remaining $5.125 million while denying a capital-call order, cover damages and Vale's fees.
summary.core_legal_issue: Whether Gray Jay's obligation under the ECL to buy up to $8 million more in Vale securities, triggered as the VPN was repaid, terminated automatically before it arose, either through a "default and acceleration of the [VPN]" or through Vale's "insolvency", or was excused by a prior material breach of the implied covenant or by frustration of purpose. The VPN was repaid in full by PWS in the Pilot Transaction, a deal Vale deliberately structured downstream of Vale to avoid tripping the ECL's termination conditions. The opinion also decides what remedy follows.
summary.disposition: granted in part and denied in part
summary.holding: Judgment for Vale on Count I (breach of the ECL); Vale's Count II (implied covenant) fails as waived and on the merits. Gray Jay did not prove that the ECL terminated before its obligation arose. The Court did not resolve whether a VPN default occurred, which turned on whether PWS paid before or after closing, because there was no acceleration: PWS's payment was a § 2.03(a) prepayment, the OWL Lender never declared the VPN due, and the prevention doctrine does not apply. Gray Jay also failed to prove balance-sheet or cash-flow insolvency at the time of the Pilot Transaction. Its excuse defenses (prior material breach of the implied covenant and frustration of purpose) fail, and its requested adverse inference is denied as moot. Remedy: Gray Jay is ordered to specifically perform its remaining $5.125 million investment obligation, but the Court will not order a capital call. Damages for interest on the Oceanides Promissory Note are denied because the ECL's $10 million cap leaves no room for them, so the Court did not decide whether they are consequential. Vale is awarded costs but denied attorneys' fees under the bad-faith exception: Gray Jay won intermediate victories, its defenses were cognizable and the Madera argument was not entirely frivolous, and Vale's own incomplete document collection weighed against shifting. Gray Jay's request for the fees it incurred on its spoliation motion is granted based on Vale's at least negligent failure to preserve Stone's and Irani's texts, and Gray Jay must file a Rule 88 affidavit. The parties must submit a proposed implementing order within ten business days and confer on a schedule for supplemental briefing on whether the ECL damages cap affects pre- and post-judgment interest.
key_facts_and_concessions: The ECL, signed only by Vale and Gray Jay, terminates Gray Jay's purchase obligation "automatically and immediately" upon, among other events, Vale's "bankruptcy or insolvency" or "any default and acceleration of the [VPN]". At summary judgment the Court held that both default and acceleration are required, that insolvency is measured at or before the funding obligation, and that Gray Jay's remaining obligation is no greater than $5.125 million (Gray Jay had already invested $4.875 million).

Vale sent the OWL Lender a Repayment Notice on September 23, 2022. The OWL Lender returned executed signature pages for the Repayment Notice and Payoff Letter on September 29, with Johnson signing as an "Authorized Person" for the OWL Lender. PWS repaid the VPN on September 30, and no one objected. It is undisputed that the OWL Lender never gave notice advancing the VPN's maturity.

Johnson testified that he and NGP, which controlled the OWL Lender, discussed whether to declare a default but chose not to "rock the boat" because they wanted their money back. Johnson also admitted he did not think the documents imposed a notice obligation regarding the Pilot Transaction.

Vale does not dispute that it deliberately structured the Pilot Transaction so the VPN was paid before any change in control or asset transfer (fn. 298). Instar had pushed for the deal to occur downstream of Vale so that no ECL change of control would occur (fn. 80).

Gray Jay did not dispute that the ECL is valid and required it to invest after VPN repayment, admitted it "declined to invest," and did not respond to Vale's breach argument. The Court deemed any response waived.

Vale's 2021 audited consolidated financials showed roughly $574 million in assets against $291 million in liabilities, and Vale's expert Ratliff opined, unrebutted, that Vale was not insolvent at the Pilot Transaction. Gray Jay offered no financial expert and relied on a July 2022 Instar slide deck comparing OWL's $263 million "Fair Market Value" with $278 million of consolidated debt.

OCD cleared the Madera Well to resume operations on January 18, 2022 and did not reopen its investigation until August 2023. Contemporaneous documents did not describe the Madera Event as a catastrophe. Gray Jay conceded that the balance-sheet impact was "difficult to estimate" and did not oppose GAAP's "probable and reasonably estimable" standard.

Vale made negligible efforts to collect text messages from Stone and Irani when they left Instar and made no effort to stop Irani from routinely deleting texts between 2020 and 2023. Vale was "certainly aware" of the need to preserve those texts by Gray Jay's January 2023 litigation-hold request (fn. 302).
summary.practical_takeaway: Investors who want an equity commitment to fall away on a sale or refinancing of the issuer's business should draft an express trigger. A condition tied to "default and acceleration" of seller debt will not be met by a negotiated prepayment, and the Court will not use the implied covenant or frustration of purpose to supply the missing protection. Plaintiffs should answer every remedy-limiting argument, such as a damages cap, in post-trial briefing, and should preserve departing custodians' texts once a dispute is foreseeable, since a negligent failure can cost fees and undercut a bad-faith fee request.
summary.standard_of_review: Post-trial; preponderance of the evidence. Vale bore the burden on its contract and implied covenant claims, and Gray Jay bore the burden on its affirmative defenses. Because the ECL's termination events extinguish an existing duty (formerly called conditions subsequent), Gray Jay, as the party seeking to avoid the obligation, bore the burden of proving them. Specific performance required clear and convincing evidence and rests in the Court's discretion.

entries.name: Peter A. Walker v. Icon Management Aggregator L.P. and Icon Topco L.P.

arguments_rejected_or_waived: Defendants' objection that the counterclaims seek damages and other relief beyond the declarations sought in the Underlying Action: rejected. Success would still defeat the Underlying Plaintiffs' asserted entitlement to acquire Walker's units on the challenged terms, so the counterclaims keep their defensive function.

Contention that the counterclaims' additional elements break the logical relationship with the Underlying Complaint: rejected. Resolving them requires examining the same agreements and the circumstances of the amendment and repurchase, and the added elements do not eliminate that factual and legal overlap.

Walker's argument that his third-party claims need not satisfy Roven because Section 6.04(f) omits "in defending" and covers anyone "made party to" or "otherwise involved in" a proceeding: rejected under Edmundson and Krauss. Neither that participation language nor Section 6.04(e)'s non-exclusive reference to investigating or defending claims exempts offensive claims from Roven.

Argument that the claims against KKR are compulsory: rejected. Rule 14(a)(1) impleader is permissive, KKR asserted no claim against Walker, and joining KKR does not make claims against it compulsory under Rule 13(a).

Argument that the third-party claims serve to defeat or offset the claims against Walker: rejected. Walker made no such showing, and as in Krauss, pleading additional claims against a previously unnamed party does not establish their defensive character.

authorities_cited.authority: Citadel Holding Corp. v. Roven, 603 A.2d 818 (Del. 1992)
authorities_cited.proposition: Two-part test for advancing counterclaim expenses; prejudgment interest is ordinarily awarded as of right and runs from the date of demand.

authorities_cited.authority: Pontone v. Milso Indus. Corp., 100 A.3d 1023 (Del. Ch. 2014) (Pontone II)
authorities_cited.proposition: A counterclaim is advanceable if it is compulsory and advanced to defeat or offset the affirmative claims; same transaction or occurrence means a logical relationship, informed by shared fact, law and evidence; a potential offsetting damages award qualifies; interest runs from the date the amount was specified and the undertaking produced.

authorities_cited.authority: Krauss v. 180 Life Scis. Corp., 2022 WL 665323 (Del. Ch. Mar. 7, 2022)
authorities_cited.proposition: "Offset" is read broadly; offensive litigation generally is not advanceable; a third-party claim against previously unnamed parties was not shown to be compulsory or defensive; Roven applied despite "otherwise participating" coverage language.

authorities_cited.authority: Edmundson v. Theorem Techs., Inc., 2026 WL 2688857, at *8 n.69 (Del. Ch. Sept. 14, 2026)
authorities_cited.proposition: Omitting "in defending" language does not by itself dispense with Roven's requirements; the Court noted that Report is on exceptions before a constitutionally appointed member of the court (fn. 53).

authorities_cited.authority: Pontone v. Milso Indus. Corp., 2014 WL 2439973 (Del. Ch. May 29, 2014) (Pontone I)
authorities_cited.proposition: Roven made a counterclaim advanceable because recovery would offset liability even though it could not defeat the claim; a broad reading of offset comports with Delaware policy favoring advancement.

authorities_cited.authority: Partnership Agreement § 6.04(f)
authorities_cited.proposition: Mandatory advancement for an Indemnitee made party to or otherwise involved in a proceeding, upon a written undertaking to repay.

authorities_cited.authority: Partnership Agreement § 6.04(e)
authorities_cited.proposition: Indemnification scope; its reference to investigating or defending claims does not exempt offensive claims from Roven.

authorities_cited.authority: Fed. R. Civ. P. 13(a)(1); Ct. Ch. R. 13(a)
authorities_cited.proposition: A counterclaim is compulsory if it arises out of the transaction or occurrence that is the subject of the opposing party's claim, and Rule 13(a) reaches only an opposing party.
Impleader of a nonparty is permissive, not required, so third-party claims are not compulsory.

authorities_cited.authority: Transamerica Occidental Life Ins. Co. v. Aviation Off. of Am., Inc., 292 F.3d 384 (3d Cir. 2002)
authorities_cited.proposition: The logical-relationship requirement is viewed liberally to promote judicial economy.

authorities_cited.authority: Leiske v. Kidd, 2026 WL 265493 (Del. Ch. Feb. 2, 2026) (citing Stifel Fin. Corp. v. Cochran, 809 A.2d 555 (Del. 2002))
authorities_cited.proposition: Fees-on-fees in proportion to success is the default rule absent contrary contract language.
Prejudgment interest at the legal rate.

authorities_cited.authority: Danenberg v. Fitracks, Inc., 58 A.3d 991 (Del. Ch. 2012)
authorities_cited.proposition: Model fee-dispute resolution plan to be included in the proposed implementing order.

authorities_cited.authority: Mooney v. Echo Therapeutics, Inc., 2015 WL 3413272 (Del. Ch. May 28, 2015)
authorities_cited.proposition: Quoted through Krauss: offensive litigation is generally not advanceable.

authorities_cited.authority: Fasciana v. Elec. Data Sys. Corp., 829 A.2d 178 (Del. Ch. 2003)
authorities_cited.proposition: Additional support for fees-on-fees.

authorities_cited.authority: Rhodes v. bioMerieux, Inc., 2024 WL 669034 (Del. Ch. Feb. 19, 2024); Senior Tour Players 207 Mgmt. Co. LLC v. Golftown 207 Hldg. Co., LLC, 853 A.2d 124 (Del. Ch. 2004)
authorities_cited.proposition: Summary judgment suits advancement disputes, which are resolved on the plain meaning of the governing instruments.

authorities_cited.authority: Cianciulli v. Webinar.Net, Inc., 2025 WL 2831336 (Del. Ch. Oct. 6, 2025); Ct. Ch. R. 56(c)(3); D.R.E. 202(d)(1)
authorities_cited.proposition: The Court may take judicial notice of filings in the Underlying Action.

authorities_cited.authority: Ct. Ch. R. 56(a)
authorities_cited.proposition: Summary judgment standard.

authorities_cited.authority: Partnership Agreement § 6.03
authorities_cited.proposition: Topco must pay or cause to be paid the Partnership's obligations, including those under Section 6.04.
Governs the deadline for exceptions to the Report.

summary.brief_summary: Walker, Instructure's former CFO, sued the Partnership and Topco for advancement under Section 6.04(f) of the Partnership Agreement for the Underlying Action, in which the Underlying Plaintiffs seek to validate the Call Right Amendment and the $0 Call Notice used to extinguish his vested Class C Units; the parties cross-moved for summary judgment before a Magistrate in Chancery. With defense costs and Count One conceded, the Court applied Roven and held that the remaining counterclaims against the Underlying Plaintiffs are compulsory and defensive, even though they also seek damages. Following Edmundson and Krauss, the Court held that the absence of "in defending" language does not exempt offensive claims from Roven, and that the permissive third-party claims against KKR, which asserted no claim against Walker, are neither compulsory nor defensive.
summary.core_legal_issue: Whether Section 6.04(f) of the Partnership Agreement, which covers an Indemnitee "made party to, or is otherwise involved in" a proceeding without "in defending" language, entitles Walker to advancement beyond his undisputed defense costs: specifically, for prosecuting counterclaims against the Underlying Plaintiffs and third-party claims against KKR under the Citadel Holding Corp. v. Roven compulsory-and-defensive test.
summary.disposition: granted in part and denied in part
summary.holding: Cross-motions granted in part and denied in part. Walker is entitled to advancement for defending the Underlying Action, which is undisputed. He is also entitled to advancement for Counterclaims One, Two, Five, Seven, Eight, Nine and Ten insofar as asserted against the Underlying Plaintiffs: Count One is conceded, and the rest satisfy both Roven prongs because they bear a logical relationship to the declaratory claims and would defeat the Underlying Plaintiffs' asserted entitlement to acquire his units on the challenged terms. He is not entitled to advancement for his third-party claims against KKR (Counts Three, Four and Six, and Counts Seven, Eight and Ten as asserted against KKR). Section 6.04(f)'s broad participation language does not displace Roven, impleader under Rule 14(a)(1) is permissive, KKR asserted no claim against him, and he did not show those claims defeat or offset the claims against him. Walker receives fees-on-fees to the extent of his success and prejudgment interest at the legal rate from the date of demand. Exceptions are due by October 26, 2026. If none are taken or the Report is affirmed, the parties must meet and confer within five business days and submit a proposed implementing order with a Danenberg v. Fitracks-style fee-dispute plan.
key_facts_and_concessions: Defendants do not dispute Walker's entitlement to advancement for defending against their claims in the Underlying Action (fn. 32), so only the counterclaims and third-party claims were contested.
Defendants concede that Counterclaim Count One is advanceable (fn. 39).

The Underlying Action, brought by the Partnership, Topco, Instructure and Topco GP (the "Underlying Plaintiffs"), seeks declarations that the Call Right Amendment and the Call Notice are valid and enforceable; it arises from the repurchase of Walker's vested Class C Units for no consideration (a purported fair market value of $0) after his resignation.

Counterclaims Two, Five, Seven, Eight, Nine and Ten each challenge the same amendment and repurchase the Underlying Plaintiffs seek to validate, sounding respectively in fiduciary duty, contract, conversion, unjust enrichment, implied covenant and promissory estoppel.
KKR asserted no claim against Walker; Walker joined KKR as a third-party defendant, alleging KKR controlled Defendants and its employees directed the challenged conduct.

Section 6.04(f) mandates advancement for an Indemnitee who "was, is or is threatened to be made party to, or is otherwise involved in" a proceeding, upon a written undertaking, and does not limit coverage to expenses incurred "in defending."
Neither side filed the Underlying Complaint or Underlying Counterclaims in this record, but the Court took judicial notice of them (fn. 18).
Walker qualifies as an Indemnitee through his service as an employee/officer and his status as a former or current Partner (fn. 35).
summary.practical_takeaway: Broad "made party to or otherwise involved in" advancement language will not, by itself, carry impleader claims against a non-adverse party such as a controller, so claimants should be ready to show both Roven prongs for every claim against every defendant. Counterclaims that attack the very transaction a declaratory plaintiff seeks to validate remain advanceable even when they also seek damages.
summary.standard_of_review: Ct. Ch. R. 56(a) summary judgment on cross-motions (no genuine dispute of material fact; entitlement to judgment as a matter of law), applying the plain meaning of the advancement provisions; counterclaim and third-party advanceability measured by the two-part Roven test. Issued as a Magistrate's Report under Ct. Ch. R. 144, subject to exceptions.
